name: Dry Creek Route
approach: From the Big Four Picnic Area / Ice Caves Trailhead (1,640 ft) on the Mountain Loop Highway, follow the paved nature-trail toward the ice caves, then leave the trail to cross the South Fork Stillaguamish River on a fallen log. Travel southeasterly through open forest roughly a mile to reach Dry Creek, then ascend through the lower basin -- in snow conditions via a hidden snow chute, in bare conditions via a series of class 3-4 ledges and ramps -- into the upper basin. From the upper basin, traverse the exposed red slabs to gain the east ridge below the couloir/gully system that leads to the summit ridge.

climbing_route.label: Exposed red slabs to the east ridge
climbing_route.notes: From the upper basin, traverse the exposed red slabs to gain the east ridge below the couloir/gully system.

climbing_route.label: Couloir/gully system to the summit ridge
climbing_route.notes: The couloir/gully system above the east ridge leads to the summit ridge.

pitch_detail.notes: Log crossing of the South Fork Stillaguamish River, then travel through open forest to the Dry Creek basin
Series of ledges and ramps in the lower basin; deep moats with thin, unsupportive snow overhangs possible where snow meets rock
Exposed traverse of red slabs to reach the east ridge
Follow the summit ridge over the lower (first) bump to the true summit (second, higher bump)

itinerary: A single long day from the trailhead: hike the approach trail/road to the Dry Creek basin, ascend the gully/ledges and red-slab traverse to the east ridge, follow the summit ridge to the true summit, then reverse via the south-ridge rappel and downclimb back to the basin and trailhead.
overview: Big Four's standard/easiest line: a long, steep approach up the Dry Creek basin on the mountain's east side, followed by a gully and an exposed traverse of red slabs to the east ridge, then the summit ridge to the true (higher, second) summit bump. There is no easy way up this peak -- even the 'standard' route involves sustained class 3-4 scrambling, a committing couloir, and a technical rappel/downclimb on the way out.
